newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia Treasury urges bank competition.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia Treasury urges bank competition.

text.p: Australia's Federal Treasury said it has recommended removal of the prohibition on foreign ownership of Australia's four major banks as a means of enhancing competition in the Australian banking market.
The recommendation is contained in the Treasury's submission to the Wallis financial system inquiry, Treasury Secretary Ted Evans said in a speech entitled "The Evolving Financial System.

"The removal of the prohibition on foreign ownership of Australia's four major banks is (also) raised for consideration as this may assist in enhancing the competitive pressures in the Australian banking market," Evans said in his speech.

Evans also said Treasury had recommended amalgamating the Reserve Bank's prudential functions with those of the Australian Financial Institutions Commission (AFIC), whose responsibilities included building societies and credit unions.
"Treasury also sees merit in combining the Australian Securities Commission (ASC) and the Insurance and Superannuation Commission (ISC) into a single regulatory body," he said.

Evans also raised the possibility of separate regulators with specific responsibilities for aspects of the financial system, reporting to a common "board" responsible for the efficient supervision of all the financial system.

Rather than maintaining the current prohibition on mergers between the larger banks and life offices, Treasury would rather see competition concerns left for the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) to determine, Evans said.
"In doing so, however, any definition of the 'market' for financial services should recognise the globalisation of the financial system," he said.

Treasury had additionally raised the possibility of establishing an advisory panel of representatives drawn from industry participants to be responsible for monitoring the financial regulation system to ensure it remained up to date.
Evans said he was disappointed at submissions put so far to the Wallis inquiry which is due to report to the Federal Government by March next year.
"For some, the focus appears to be on putting a case for maintaining the status quo or for only some minor fine tuning," he said.

"It might also be considered disappointing that parts of the industry appear to lack the necessary confidence to take advantage of the opportunities that would emerge from ensuring the ongoing efficiency and competitiveness of the financial system," Evans said.
Evans said he stressed that Treasury was not advocating the end of prudential supervision of financial institutions - "prudential regulation is a sine qua non."

Evans said consumers will have to become more discriminating in their dealings with banks. "And banks will have to disclose the necessary information for the market to form judgements, not just about products but their ability to offer those products on an ongoing basis," he said.
Evans said removing the requirement for the Reserve Bank to protect bank depositors "would be a step forward toward helping to change perceptions of the special status of banks.
"All savers, including savers in superannuation schemes, will have to accept more responsibility for their investment decisions," Evans said.
The Treasury submission also suggested the move to market value and risk accounting for financial institutions, away from the current historical cost accounting framework, Evans said.
"We (also) believe the preferred way to regulate financial conglomerates is through a holding company structure," he said.
Evan said Treasury's recommendations did not advocate an abrupt change in approach to financial system regulation.
"To the extent that there has been talk of 'evolution' rather than 'revolution', we are firmly in the evolution camp," Evans said.
-- Sydney newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
